Feels obligatory to test Claude Fable 5’s performance in game development.

I fed it an old rougelike HTML action game I previously built with Opus, and Fable 5 turned it into 3D in 10 minutes.

The upgrade is obvious

- Animation
Before: Nano Banana + motion frame generator + ASCII converter to get usable action sprites and animation.
After: prompt directly generates the weapon and matched animation.

- Audio Design
Before: only one basic hit sound repeated.
After: BGM, hit SFX, enemy kill SFX, and level clear audio.

- Visual
Before: ASCII visuals were mostly flat and hard to push into action gameplay.
After: it preserved the 2D ASCII aesthetic, while adding 3D depth, perspective, and impact through a hybrid rendering style.

- Character
Before: even simple boss designs like a spider or tiger were hard to recreate.
After: it pulled boss prototypes from my design doc, turned them into 3D models, and animated them in one pass.

The attacks also feel much better, though I’m not 100% sure how much of that comes from my earlier stat tweaks versus Fable itself.

This is the real intent-to-gameplay moment.

Claude Fable 5 just changed the AI game.

People are one-shotting games, 3D worlds, app builders and insane code optimizations.  There's a major shift.

For three years we've used AI to answer questions but this one does the work itself.

Stripe gave it a fifty-million-line codebase to migrate, two months of work for a team. Done in a day.

I've spent years paying specialists a fortune for work this now does by the hour. The options traders, engineers and analysts you used to need a war chest to afford.

And Anthropic showed how far it really goes....

The unrestricted version was SO good at finding security flaws across the world's software that they refused to release it, handed it to the people guarding critical infrastructure, and gave everyone else a version with the dangerous parts walled off.

We're building toward an economy where software moves money on its own and settles deals with no human in the loop. That only stands up if the code underneath can't be broken, and we just got the most powerful tool ever made for finding what is.

Anthropic's line at launch was "point it at something that matters."

That's the whole game now.

The model is the same for everyone who signs up.

The edge was never the tool. It's taste, conviction, and knowing what's worth building.

What a time.

data.text:
CLAUDE FABLE 5 "FIND ME A PHOTO OF A SUNSET AND POST IT IN SLACK" OUT LOUD, WITH THEIR VOICE  AND WATCHED IT OPEN A BROWSER, DOWNLOAD THE IMAGE, AND POST IT. ZERO CLICKS.

this is the part of the june 9 launch nobody's talking about. everyone's posting the mario clones and the 3D websites. the real shift is that fable 5 stopped being a thing you type to

you talk. it executes a multi-step task across real apps. browser, file system, slack chained together from one spoken sentence

the benchmark story behind why it can do this:

→ 80.3% on SWE-Bench Pro. opus 4.8 sits at 69.2%, GPT-5.5 at 58.6%. an 11-point jump over anthropic's own previous best 
→ 95% on SWE-Bench Verified ahead of opus 4.8 at 88.6% and GPT-5.5 at 82.6% 
→ 29.3% on FrontierCode Diamond the hardest 50 tasks of cognition's benchmark. opus manages 13.4%, GPT-5.5 just 5.7%. more than double the previous frontier 
→ rebuilds a web app's source code from a screenshot alone. no codebase, no DOM access

the thing that makes it feel different isn't the scores. it's persistence. it stays focused across a million tokens, takes its own notes, and improves its output mid-task without being told. early partners say it "one-shots" full apps that used to need hundreds of prompts

the catches, honest version:

→ $10 per million input, $50 output. exactly double opus. long voice-agent runs add up fast 
→ prompts touching cybersecurity, bio, chem, or model distillation silently reroute to opus 4.8 
→ free on pro/max/team only until june 22. after that it's extra usage billing

a year ago AI was a thing you prompted. today it's a thing you delegate to with your voice while you make coffee

the gap between people typing one request and people running voice-driven agents across their whole stack is about to get embarrassing
